AUTH-01.story: As a trader, I can create an account with email and password on my prop firm's domain so that I belong to that firm's tenant.

AUTH-02.story: As the platform, I require new traders to verify their email before trading so that fake accounts are reduced.

AUTH-03.story: As a tenant admin, I can invite staff by email and assign a role so that they get scoped access without sharing credentials.

AUTH-04.story: As any user, I can log in with email and password and be placed in the correct tenant context from the domain so that I only see my firm's data.

AUTH-05.story: As a user, I can reset a forgotten password through a single-use email link so that I regain access securely.

AUTH-06.story: As a trader, I can sign up and log in with Google so that onboarding is faster.

AUTH-07.story: As the platform, I issue short-lived JWT access tokens with rotating refresh tokens and server-side revocation so that stolen tokens expire quickly.

AUTH-08.story: As a user, I can view my active sessions and log out of all devices so that I can remove access from a lost device.

AUTH-09.story: As a tenant admin or staff member, I must enroll TOTP two-factor at first login so that financial operations are protected.

AUTH-10.story: As a trader, I can optionally enable TOTP two-factor so that my funded account is safer.

AUTH-11.story: As a 2FA user, I receive one-time backup codes so that I am not locked out if I lose my device.

AUTH-12.story: As the platform, I define Super Admin, Tenant Admin, custom staff roles, Trader, and API Consumer so that access maps to responsibility.

AUTH-13.story: As the platform, I enforce permission keys declared by each module in resource.action format at the API layer so that modules plug in without custom auth code.

AUTH-14.story: As a tenant admin, I can create roles and assign permission subsets so that staff access matches my org structure.

AUTH-15.story: As the platform, I restrict every query and action to the caller's tenant inside the data layer so that cross-tenant access is impossible by construction.

AUTH-16.story: As a platform owner, my console identity cannot act inside a tenant except through audited impersonation so that tenant data stays protected.

AUTH-17.story: As the platform, I enforce minimum strength and hash with argon2id so that credentials resist offline cracking.

AUTH-18.story: As the platform, I rate limit login attempts and lock accounts after repeated failures so that credential stuffing fails.

AUTH-19.story: As a user and as an admin, I can see recent logins with device and location so that suspicious access is visible.

AUTH-20.story: As a tenant admin, I can suspend a user so that all their sessions and tokens are invalidated immediately.

AUTH-21.story: As a tenant admin, I can issue, rotate, and revoke API keys for BYO integrations so that external systems authenticate without user credentials.

AUTH-22.story: As the platform, I log every login, failed login, password change, role change, and key rotation to the audit log so that security events are traceable.

AUTH-23.story: As a tenant admin on an enterprise plan, I can restrict staff logins to approved IP ranges so that office-only access is enforced.

AUTH-24.story: As a tenant admin on enterprise plan, I can configure SAML/OIDC SSO so that my staff uses corporate identity providers.

AUTH-25.story: As a tenant admin, I sync users from my identity provider via SCIM so that staff onboarding is automated.

AUTH-26.story: As a trader, I can log in with magic link or WebAuthn so that I avoid password fatigue.

AUTH-27.story: As a tenant admin with permission, I force logout all sessions of a specific trader without a full suspension, so that I can respond to suspected compromise proportionally.

AUTH-28.story: As support staff with permission, I reset a trader or staff 2FA enrollment after identity checks, with audit and a cooldown on sensitive actions, so that a lost device does not permanently lock an account.

AUTH-29.story: As a user, I change my account email only through confirmation to both old and new addresses with a cooldown on payouts and full audit, so that email change cannot be used as an account takeover path.

AUTH-30.story: As the platform, I require a fresh 2FA challenge for sensitive actions such as payout method change, role change, and bulk suspension, so that a stolen session cannot perform high-risk operations.

AUTH-31.story: As the platform, I record which version of terms, privacy, and risk disclaimer each user accepted at registration and re-accept after changes, so that legal consent is provable per trader.

AUTH-32.story: As the platform, I block disposable email domains, rate limit registrations per IP , and require a bot challenge on signup, so that fake account farms become expensive to run.

AUTH-33.story: As the platform, login, password reset, and invite flows return identical responses for known and unknown emails, so that attackers cannot harvest valid accounts.

AUTH-34.story: As a tenant admin, I configure session lifetimes and remember-me policy separately for traders and staff, so that session risk matches firm policy.

AUTH-35.story: As a trader, I close my own account only when no open positions, pending payouts, or open risk cases exist, with a retention notice, so that closure is safe and compliant.

AUTH-36.story: As staff, I merge duplicate trader identities belonging to one person across multiple emails with audit and consolidated history, so that abuse analysis and CRM see one person.

AUTH-37.story: As a user, I view and revoke devices trusted for 2FA step-up exemption, so that a lost device can be untrusted remotely.

AUTH-38.story: As the platform, I enforce staff password expiry and block reused passwords, so that staff credentials meet enterprise tenant expectations.

TEN-01.story: As a super admin, I can create, view, edit, suspend, and terminate a tenant so that each prop firm has an isolated workspace.

TEN-02.story: As the platform, I resolve the tenant from the request domain or subdomain at the edge so that branding, config, and data scope are correct for every request.

TEN-03.story: As the platform, I inject the caller's tenant id into every repository query so that no module can read another tenant's rows.

TEN-04.story: As a tenant admin, I can set logo, favicon, colors, and fonts so that the trader portal and admin panel look like my brand.

TEN-05.story: As a tenant admin, I can map my own domain to my tenant so that traders see my URL instead of a platform subdomain.

TEN-06.story: As a tenant admin, I can rename core terms such as challenge, trader, and payout so that the UI speaks my firm's language.

TEN-07.story: As a tenant admin, I can set default currency, timezone, and locale so that amounts and timestamps display correctly for my market.

TEN-08.story: As a super admin, I can enable or disable modules per tenant so that each firm gets exactly the capabilities it purchased.

TEN-09.story: As the platform, I track each tenant module as installed, enabled, suspended, or disabled so that UI and APIs respect the real state.

TEN-10.story: As a super admin or a scoped tenant admin, I can toggle feature flags per tenant so that rollout is controlled per firm.

TEN-11.story: As a tenant admin, I can store my broker credentials, payment provider keys, KYC settings, and email sender config so that integrations run under my own accounts.

TEN-12.story: As the platform, I encrypt tenant integration secrets at rest and never return them in logs or API responses so that credentials stay safe.

TEN-13.story: As a tenant admin, I can set my terms, privacy policy, and risk disclaimer so that my compliance text is displayed to my traders.

TEN-14.story: As a tenant admin, I can configure my sending domain and from-address so that transactional emails arrive from my brand.

TEN-15.story: As a super admin, I can suspend a tenant so that logins, new orders, and payouts stop immediately while all data is preserved.

TEN-16.story: As a super admin, I can impersonate a tenant admin with explicit consent and full audit so that support is possible without sharing passwords.

TEN-17.story: As a frontend app, I can fetch one tenant context containing branding, entitlements, flags, and terminology at bootstrap so that the UI composes itself in a single call.

TEN-18.story: As the platform, I prefix every tenant file in object storage by tenant id so that documents and certificates never mix between firms.

TEN-19.story: As the platform, I log tenant creation, suspension, config changes, and entitlement changes with actor and timestamp so that platform-level changes are traceable.

TEN-20.story: As the platform, I record per-tenant usage counters for traders, accounts, orders, and API calls so that future billing has real data.

TEN-21.story: As a super admin, I can see per-tenant error rates and broker sync health so that I spot a failing tenant before they report it.

TEN-22.story: As a super admin, I set per-tenant limits on traders, accounts, and API calls so that resource abuse is prevented.

TEN-23.story: As a super admin, I receive alerts when tenants approach quotas so that I can upsell or intervene before limits hit.

TEN-24.story: As a tenant on regulated markets, I choose data residency region so that compliance requirements are met.

TEN-25.story: As a tenant admin, I run a connection test per configured integration including broker, payment provider, KYC provider, and email sender, and see a clear pass or fail with the provider response, so that bad credentials surface at config time instead of at first payout.

TEN-26.story: As a tenant admin, I see DNS verification status and SSL provisioning state for my custom domain with the exact records to add, so that domain cutover is self-serve and debuggable without support tickets.

TEN-27.story: As a tenant admin or platform ops, I see which settings inherit platform defaults and which are tenant overrides, with the resolved effective value, so that config behavior is never a guess during support.

TEN-28.story: As a tenant admin, I see change history for branding, terminology, and settings with diffs and can roll back to a prior version, so that a bad change is recoverable without engineering help.

TEN-29.story: As a tenant admin, when I publish a new terms or risk disclaimer version, traders must re- accept at next login or before their next payout request, and acceptance is logged per version, so that consent stays current and provable.

TEN-30.story: As a tenant admin, I follow a setup checklist covering branding, domain, broker connection test, first challenge, payment test, payout methods, and KYC config, with visible completion state, so that launch readiness is explicit for me and for platform support.

TEN-31.story: As a tenant admin, I enable or disable channels per tenant and set mandatory channels for critical events such as breach and payout, so that communication matches my operations and my compliance posture.

TEN-32.story: As a tenant admin, I see staff last active date, role, and 2FA status and can disable dormant accounts in one action, so that stale access does not accumulate over months.

TEN-33.story: As platform ops, I execute a tenant offboarding that exports traders, accounts, ledger, and audit as a defined package, then terminates entitlements while retaining data per contract, so that exits are clean and contractual.

TEN-34.story: As platform ops, I clone configuration from an existing tenant into a new tenant with explicit include and exclude choices, so that onboarding tenant two and beyond is fast and consistent.

TEN-35.story: As a super admin, before disabling a module I see affected active entities such as pending commissions, open competitions, and scheduled payouts, so that destructive commercial changes are deliberate.

TEN-36.story: As the platform, I run automated tests that attempt cross-tenant data access across every module and fail the build on any leak, so that tenant isolation is proven continuously rather than assumed.

TEN-37.story: As a tenant, I can export my complete tenant data in documented standard formats at any time, so that my data is never hostage to the platform and migration is always possible.

TEN-38.story: As the platform, I distinguish soft archival from irreversible hard deletion with enforced retention windows and audit, so that offboarding meets both operational and legal requirements.

TEN-39.story: As a tenant admin, I can preview configuration changes in a dry-run mode before applying them to production, so that risky changes are validated without needing rollback.

TEN-40.story: As platform ops, I can publish incident and maintenance notices scoped to specific affected tenants rather than platform-wide, so that communication stays relevant and calm.

EVT-01.story: As a module developer, I write domain state and an outbox row in one database transaction so that no event is lost and no event is emitted for a rolled-back transaction.

EVT-02.story: As the platform, a dedicated relay process polls the outbox and publishes events to Redis Streams so that delivery survives application restarts.

EVT-03.story: As the platform, every event carries id, type, version, tenant_id, occurred_at, and payload so that consumers can evolve safely and scope correctly.

EVT-04.story: As the platform, I maintain a versioned catalog of all domain events with producers and payload contracts so that modules agree on definitions before code is written.

EVT-05.story: As a consumer module, I deduplicate by event id so that redelivery never causes double emails, double payouts, or double ledger entries.

EVT-06.story: As the platform, each consumer module subscribes with its own consumer group so that one slow consumer never blocks the others.

EVT-07.story: As the platform, I move events to a dead letter stream with error context after a maximum retry count so that poison events never stall a pipeline.

EVT-08.story: As the platform, I persist every published event to an append-only log table so that replay and audit are always possible.

EVT-09.story: As the platform, I can replay events from the event log to rebuild a read model or recover a consumer so that recovery needs no production hacks.

EVT-10.story: As a module owner, I use shared utilities to verify provider signatures and deduplicate by provider event id so that payment and KYC webhooks are handled consistently and idempotently.

EVT-11.story: As a tenant admin, I can register webhook URLs per event type so that my external checkout, CRM, or affiliate system reacts to platform events.

EVT-12.story: As the platform, I sign every outbound webhook with HMAC using a per-tenant secret so that receivers can verify authenticity.

EVT-13.story: As the platform, I retry failed webhook deliveries with exponential backoff and a maximum attempt count so that transient receiver outages do not lose events.

EVT-14.story: As a tenant admin, I can view delivery attempts, response codes, and payloads so that I can debug my own integration without asking support.

EVT-15.story: As a tenant admin, I can send a test event to my endpoint so that I can validate my integration before going live.

EVT-16.story: As the platform, I throttle deliveries per endpoint and open a circuit breaker on repeated failures so that one broken endpoint cannot consume all workers.

EVT-17.story: As the notifications module, I consume lifecycle events so that emails and in-app alerts fire without any producer calling me directly.

EVT-18.story: As the reports module, I consume events to maintain read models so that analytics never query operational tables.

EVT-19.story: As the platform, every event carries tenant_id and every consumer enforces tenant scope so that cross-tenant leakage through events is impossible.

EVT-20.story: As the platform, I keep broker commands in a separate Postgres command table with retry and backoff so that commands, which are requests, are never confused with events, which are facts.

EVT-21.story: As ops, I get alerts on outbox lag, consumer lag, and dead letter growth so that pipeline problems surface before traders notice.

EVT-22.story: As the platform, I age out Redis Streams and archive the event log so that storage stays bounded without losing replay history.

EVT-23.story: As the platform, I maintain a versioned schema registry with validation so that event contracts are enforced.

EVT-24.story: As a consumer, I subscribe to filtered event streams so that I only receive relevant events.

EVT-25.story: As the platform, I guarantee that all events for a single entity (account, order, payout) are processed by consumers in emission order, so that state transitions never race (e.g., breach processed before account-created).

EVT-26.story: As the platform, I validate inbound webhook timestamps (reject if older than 5 minutes) and track processed event IDs to reject duplicates, so that captured webhook payloads cannot be replayed by attackers.

EVT-27.story: As ops, I can view dead letter events with error context, filter by consumer group and error type, and selectively retry or discard them, so that poison events are diagnosed and recovered without production hacks.
EVT-27.feat: Dead letter inspection and reprocessing UI

EVT-28.story: As ops, given a triggering event ID, I can trace every downstream consumer that processed it, their processing duration, and success or failure, so that multi-hop event flows are debuggable end to end.

EVT-29.story: As ops, I track per-consumer-group latency from event emission to successful processing, with configurable SLA thresholds and alerts on breach, so that slow consumers are caught before they cascade.

EVT-30.story: As the platform, I route critical events (breach, enforcement, payout approval) through a high-priority stream that cannot be starved by analytical or notification events, so that money-impacting processing is never delayed by volume spikes.

EVT-31.story: As the platform, I track per-endpoint success rate, average latency, and consecutive failures, auto-disable endpoints after sustained failure, and alert the tenant admin, so that broken integrations surface without manual checks.

EVT-32.story: As the platform, CI runs automated compatibility tests on every event schema change verifying no existing consumer breaks, so that schema evolution never silently breaks downstream modules.

GW-01.story: As the platform, I expose one API with trader, admin, console, and webhook route groups so that surface separation is enforced at the routing layer.

GW-02.story: As the platform, I resolve the tenant from the request domain or subdomain and reject unknown hosts so that no request ever executes without tenant context.

GW-03.story: As the platform, I verify JWTs or API keys on every protected route and reject invalid credentials so that anonymous access is impossible.

GW-04.story: As the platform, I enforce module-declared permission keys per route so that a user only reaches routes their role allows.

GW-05.story: As the platform, I apply per-IP and per-user rate limits with clear 429 responses so that abuse and runaway clients cannot degrade the platform.

GW-06.story: As the platform, I apply per-tenant API quotas so that one tenant cannot starve the others.

GW-07.story: As the platform, I serve per-tenant CORS policies from tenant config so that only the tenant's own domains can call the API from a browser.

GW-08.story: As the platform, I version all routes under v1 so that breaking changes ship as new versions without breaking existing tenants.

GW-09.story: As the platform, I assign a correlation id to every request and propagate it to logs, traces, and events so that any incident is traceable end to end.

GW-10.story: As ops, I get structured logs with tenant id, user id, route, status, and duration, with PII excluded, so that debugging and audit are possible.

GW-11.story: As the platform, I expose dedicated webhook endpoints for payment and KYC providers, isolated from user routes, with signature verification delegated to module utilities.

GW-12.story: As a client, I can send an idempotency key on mutating requests so that a retry after a timeout never double-creates an order, payout, or account.

GW-13.story: As the platform, I enforce maximum body size and per-route timeouts so that oversized or slow requests cannot exhaust workers.

GW-14.story: As ops and the orchestrator, I can probe liveness and readiness so that deploys and restarts are safe and traffic shifts only to healthy instances.

GW-15.story: As a developer or tenant integrator, I get an auto-generated OpenAPI spec per route group so that integration work is self-serve.

GW-16.story: As a tenant machine client, I authenticate with a tenant API key scoped to permitted routes so that integrations never use user sessions.

GW-17.story: As the platform, I mark sensitive routes such as payout approval, rule changes, and role changes for mandatory audit logging so that critical actions are always recorded.

GW-18.story: As a client, I receive a consistent error envelope with code, message, and correlation id so that all three frontends handle failures uniformly.

GW-19.story: As a tenant developer, I can call a sandbox tenant with test data so that I can integrate without touching production.

GW-20.story: As the platform, I rely on Cloudflare for WAF, DDoS, and bot mitigation and restrict origin access so that edge and app layers do not duplicate controls.

GW-21.story: As a client, every list endpoint returns cursor-based pagination with a next cursor and consistent shape, so that trader, account, payout, and ticket lists paginate uniformly and no list grows unbounded.

GW-22.story: As the platform, I check the tenant's module entitlements before routing so that routes for disabled modules return a clean 404 and tenants only reach capabilities they purchased.

GW-23.story: As the platform, I reject all mutating requests from suspended tenants while allowing read- only access, so that the TEN-15 suspension cascade is enforced at the gateway and suspended firms cannot write data.

GW-24.story: As the platform, I set cache headers on tenant context and challenge catalog responses and invalidate them when tenant config or entitlements change, so that bootstrap is fast and never serves stale branding or stale access.

GW-25.story: As a client, I submit batch mutations with a defined maximum size and receive partial- failure responses with per-item status, so that bulk operations like payout approval and account actions are atomic per item and auditable.

GW-26.story: As the platform, I provide a standardized multipart and streaming upload contract with size and type limits for KYC documents and support attachments, so that file endpoints are consistent and safe.

GW-27.story: As ops, I define explicit PII fields per route and enforce scrubbing rules in request logs, so that GW-10 structured logging never leaks emails, identity data, or payment data.

GW-28.story: As the platform, I emit Sunset and Deprecation headers on versioned routes and publish a sunset schedule, so that integrators are warned before breaking changes and the SDK-15 changelog stays accurate.

GW-29.story: As the platform, I include Retry-After headers on 429 responses and document backoff behavior, so that clients and webhooks retry predictably instead of hammering the API.

GW-30.story: As a client, every successful response uses a consistent data envelope matching the error contract in GW-18, so that frontends and integrators parse responses uniformly.

GW-31.story: As the platform, I define idempotency key expiry, tenant scope, and storage, so that GW- 12 idempotency keys do not grow unbounded and cannot collide across tenants.

GW-32.story: As the platform, I return a branded maintenance response when CON-16 maintenance mode is active, with read-only pass-through where configured, so that planned downtime is enforced at the gateway.

OPS-01.story: As the platform, every service including api, workers, relay, bot, and frontends runs as a Docker image built in CI so that all environments are identical.

OPS-02.story: As DevOps, I run production as a defined Compose stack on Hetzner so that deployment is reproducible without Kubernetes overhead.

OPS-03.story: As a developer, every push runs lint, typecheck, unit tests, and image build so that broken code never reaches main.

OPS-04.story: As DevOps, merging to main deploys to staging automatically and production deploys only via manual approval so that releases are controlled.

OPS-05.story: As the team, I have dev, staging, and production with identical configuration shape so that bugs surface before production.

OPS-06.story: As the platform, I run versioned migrations with expand-contract discipline so that schema changes never cause downtime.

OPS-07.story: As DevOps, I take daily backups plus WAL archiving and rehearse a restore monthly so that data loss is bounded and proven recoverable.

OPS-08.story: As DevOps, I enable versioning and off-host copies for KYC documents and certificates so that files are recoverable.

OPS-09.story: As DevOps, I keep secrets out of code and inject them at runtime from an encrypted store so that a repository leak is not a production leak.

OPS-10.story: As ops, I run Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and OpenTelemetry collection so that metrics, logs, and traces live in one place.

OPS-11.story: As ops, I get alerts on outbox lag, dead letter growth, reconciliation mismatch, broker sync failure, and host saturation so that we know before traders do.

OPS-12.story: As ops and tech lead, I see Grafana dashboards for sync lag, breach rate, payout queue depth, and API latency so that system health is visible at a glance.

OPS-13.story: As DevOps, I enforce SSH keys only, host firewall, fail2ban, and unattended security upgrades so that the attack surface stays small.

OPS-14.story: As DevOps, CI scans images and dependencies for vulnerabilities so that known CVEs do not ship to production.

OPS-15.story: As DevOps, I terminate TLS at Cloudflare and restrict origin access so that traffic cannot bypass the edge.

OPS-16.story: As DevOps, I deploy api, worker-realtime, worker-batch, outbox-relay, and telegram-bot as separate services with restart policies so that a stuck job cannot take down the API.

OPS-17.story: As the platform, I run scheduled jobs for sync, reconciliation, reports, and SLA checks through a defined scheduler with logs and alerts on missed runs.

OPS-18.story: As DevOps, I deploy with proxy-level switching and health gates so that traders see no interruption during releases.

OPS-19.story: As the team, staging connects to a broker sandbox so that trading flows are testable end to end before production.

OPS-20.story: As DevOps, I limit production access to named people with an audited break-glass procedure so that prod access is exceptional and logged.

OPS-21.story: As the migration team, I have import pipelines with checksums and reconciliation reports so that TTS data moves verifiably and provably.

OPS-22.story: As DevOps, I maintain a disaster recovery runbook with defined RPO and RTO and rehearse it twice a year so that recovery is practiced, not improvised.

OPS-23.story: As the business, I get alerts on Hetzner and provider spend anomalies so that infrastructure cost stays visible.

OPS-24.story: As the team, I can see deploy history and the current version per environment so that which version is live is never a guess.

OPS-25.story: As the platform, I run PgBouncer in front of Postgres with per-service pool sizing so that the API and workers never exhaust connections during sync bursts or deploy spikes.

OPS-26.story: As the platform, I configure Redis with AOF persistence for Streams and maxmemory eviction for cache use so that a restart never loses queued events or breaks rate limiting.

OPS-27.story: As the platform, scheduled jobs acquire a distributed lock so that reconciliation, reports, and detectors run exactly once across worker instances.

OPS-28.story: As the team, I follow a documented incident process with severity definitions, an on-call owner, communication steps, and mandatory postmortems for SEV-1 and SEV-2 so that incidents are handled consistently instead of ad hoc.

OPS-29.story: As the team, I run load tests against checkout, sync, evaluation, and payout paths at target volumes before cutover so that bottlenecks surface before real traders hit them.

OPS-30.story: As DevOps, I maintain a tested rollback path for every deploy with automatic rollback on failed health gates so that a bad release recovers in minutes.

OPS-31.story: As ops, I run independent uptime probes against API and frontend endpoints outside the platform so that a total outage is detected even when the platform itself is down.

OPS-32.story: As ops, I enforce log retention windows, access control, and periodic PII redaction checks so that logs stay useful, bounded, and safe.

OPS-33.story: As DevOps, I decide and document the failover approach, single instance plus rehearsed restore versus warm standby, and rehearse switchover so that database loss recovery is honest rather than assumed.

OPS-34.story: As the team, I generate synthetic traders, accounts, and orders for staging and never copy production PII so that staging is realistic and safe.

OPS-35.story: As ops, I monitor custom domain DNS and SSL expiry per tenant and alert before expiry so that no tenant goes dark silently.
